Jay-Z once stood among Colin Kaepernick's most visible celebrity allies. Now, Kaepernick sees the rapper as another powerful figure trying to revise the meaning of a choice that still follows him.

That history gives their growing feud more weight than a routine exchange between famous men. During a July concert, Jay-Z criticized Kaepernick while defending himself against backlash over his Target partnership. The retailer has faced a boycott from Black consumers since retreating from its DEI commitments.

"Buddy took a check, I ain't even mad at him, but along with that check you have to sign a non-disparagement," Jay-Z rapped, referring to Kaepernick's 2019 settlement with the NFL. "I'm the one [the NFL] can't control."

Kaepernick told NBC News that claim was false. He said his settlement did not include such an agreement. More importantly, he challenged the image Jay-Z constructed: one man supposedly silenced by a payout, the other too independent for the league to contain.

Jay-Z's old support makes his reversal harder to ignore

In 2017, Jay-Z dedicated "The Story of O.J." to Kaepernick and later wore his jersey during a "Saturday Night Live" appearance. On the 2018 song "Apes -- ," he boasted about refusing the Super Bowl because the league needed him more than he needed it.

Then came the pivot.

Roc Nation entered a partnership with the NFL in 2019, taking responsibility for the Super Bowl halftime show while also working with the league on social justice projects. Jay-Z defended the agreement by declaring that society had advanced beyond the kneeling phase and needed action.

So I am hanging out on Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace on Wednesday morning, a few minutes after calling out Dick's Sporting Goods (DKS) on Instagram for its horrific earnings day this week.

I randomly check the stock price of fellow big box retailer Target (TGT), only to find it had an ugly session the day before. It caught my attention because the broader market had hung in there, and I didn't see any analyst downgrades on Target.

I then came across something on Target with the word "backlash" in it.

"What the hell did this company do now?" I muttered to myself.

It wasn't hard to find out. Target apologized this week for selling a kids' circus clown Halloween costume that critics said evoked racist minstrel imagery. The orange-and-black costume, which included gloves, a top hat, and a mask resembling a smiling mouth with large teeth, was removed from the website, but not before consumers took Target to task.

"We removed an offensive Halloween costume that should never have been part of our assortment," Target said in a statement. "It is no longer for sale. As a company, we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry. We know this is especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners. Removing the costume is an important first step, and we are looking closely at how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this won't happen again."

The thing is, Target didn't just get this wrong. It has gotten a lot of things wrong over the past few years. Remember the 2023 Pride merchandise backlash? How about the January 2025 DEI rollback initiatives?

All of this is getting absurd, and investors need to be asking tough questions of management. Frankly, so do the Wall Street analysts who cover Target, because it's weighing on the business and could damage the valuation over time.

Consumers have more power at their fingertips than ever before -- they can take to social media to air grievances or shop at other websites to buy stuff -- and I think Target's stock falling on this news is evidence of that.

Are Target's internal product audit systems broken? Is some kind of detection software not functioning correctly? Are the hiring processes for corporate employees dysfunctional? Are corporate employees disgruntled because of big layoffs under the new CEO? Are long-tenured employees mailing it in?

What is structurally wrong inside of this retail giant that decisions like these get made time and time again? Whatever the issue, it has to be fixed by the newish executives running the company. We don't see these things happening at Costco (COST)!
title: Come on, Target. Do better.

Viola Davis is calling on Target to do more than just apologize after the retailer pulled a children's Halloween costume that critics said evoked racist Blackface and minstrel imagery.

The Oscar-winning actress rejected Target's public response in an Instagram post on Tuesday, arguing that removing the product does not address the broader harm associated with imagery that has historically dehumanized Black people.

"Target, I do not accept your apology and I do not believe that you understand the impact...the pain...the dehumanisation of the above," Davis wrote, adding, "these images laid the foundation and the ideology for every atrocity that has been committed against my people. Following criticism online, Target removed the listing.

"As a company, we know we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry," Target said in a statement. "The costume is offensive and should never have been part of our assortment. It is no longer available for sale."

The retailer also acknowledged the impact on the Black community, saying the incident was "especially hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners." The retail giant added that it was examining "how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this won't happen again." Target has also faced continued criticism over its rollback of diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. Deloitte's US settlement over alleged DEI-linked hiring and promotion raises a question: will global companies rethink how they approach diversity across their Indian workforce?

Deloitte has agreed to pay $21.5 million to settle a US Department of Justice (DOJ) investigation into its DEI (Diversity, Equity, Inclusion) practices. The DOJ alleged that Deloitte used race and sex in some hiring, promotion and staffing decisions while pursuing internal workforce targets. Deloitte has denied wrongdoing, and the settlement does not amount to an admission of liability.

The Deloitte case raises a question for multinational companies operating in India: if demographic targets are becoming a legal risk in the US, will companies rethink how they approach diversity hiring and promotions across their global workforce?

What Happened At Deloitte?

The dispute centres on how Deloitte monitored and pursued the racial and gender composition of its workforce.

The US government alleged that Deloitte had non-public demographic goals and that business units received regular updates tracking progress against them. The DOJ also alleged that some senior executives' performance evaluations were linked partly to their contribution towards meeting those workforce goals. For roughly two years, the compensation of around 150 senior Partners, Principals and Managing Directors could also have been affected if their business units failed to meet demographic targets, according to the allegations.

The government further alleged that race and sex influenced some promotion and staffing decisions and that access to certain programmes was restricted based on those characteristics.

Deloitte disputes the allegations. The company said it settled to avoid the cost, uncertainty and distraction of prolonged litigation. Of the $21.5 million settlement, around $10 million will go towards restitution, with the rest covering civil penalties and interest. A related whistle-blower claim brought by the American Alliance for Equal Rights will receive $4.3 million, according to the DOJ.

The significance of the case therefore lies not simply in the amount Deloitte is paying, but in the legal question at its centre: when does an effort to improve representation cross the line into unlawful discrimination?

Why Is Corporate DEI Under Pressure In The US?

Deloitte's settlement is part of a much wider shift in the US. The Trump administration has aggressively challenged DEI programmes, arguing that some of them can be discriminatory and undermine merit-based decision-making. The administration has also directed federal contractors and subcontractors to eliminate DEI practices.

The Justice Department created its Civil Rights Fraud Initiative in 2025 to pursue alleged discrimination linked to federal contracts. Target has removed a Halloween costume after facing criticism that it resembled blackface and racist minstrel show imagery. According to People, the company also issued a public apology. "An apology from us: We removed an offensive Halloween costume that should never have been part of our assortment," Target wrote in a statement shared on social media. "It is no longer for sale. As a company, we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry."

The costume, sold as "Kids' Glows under Blacklight Circus Clown," was modeled by a young Black boy in a black-and-orange printed bodysuit and hood with an exaggerated smile and mini top hat. The model's pose, with one leg and arm raised in a wave, was tied to Jim Crow-era depictions of Black people, as reported by The Cut.

Comedian LaTrez Anderson called it "a new low" in a now-deleted Instagram Reel about the costume, per that outlet. "The amount of people this costume had to go through to get approved says a lot. What year is it?!" one Instagram user wrote on Target's apology post.

Here's what the pose was actually referencing

Blackface is defined as dark makeup worn to mimic a Black person's appearance, often to mock or ridicule Black people, according to Merriam-Webster. The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture traces its use in the US to minstrel shows, where white performers wore blackface to mock Black people through negative stereotypes.

The character named Jim Crow, created in the 1830s by performer Thomas Dartmouth Rice, became one of the most widely repeated of these caricatures, depicting Black people as lazy, ignorant, and dependent on white slaveholders, a stereotype used to help justify slavery itself. Retailers have faced real legal consequences over blackface-linked merchandise before.

According to NBC News, Prada reached a 2020 settlement with New York City's Commission on Human Rights after a 2018 store display featured figurines with blackface imagery, in what the city called the first case holding a fashion brand legally responsible for its own product imagery. The agreement required Prada to provide recurring racial equity training to its US and Milan staff, appoint a dedicated diversity officer, and fund a scholarship program for underrepresented designers, all enforceable for six years.

The controversy comes about a year after Target scaled back its diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives. CEO Brian Cornell stepped down soon after, ending an 11-year run with the company, the outlet reported in August 2025. Target has faced consumer boycotts tied to the DEI rollback since early last year.

Anne and Lucy Dayton, daughters of one of Target's co-founders, called the company's actions "a betrayal" at the time.

Advertising for the since-deleted costume featured a black child dressed in an orange-and-black clown or jester-like suit, complete with a huge grin and hat sewn in. Advertisement

The controversy comes as the Minneapolis-based retailer continues to face scrutiny from black shoppers following its rollback of diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives.

Target announced in January 2025 that it was scaling back on several DEI efforts, including programs designed to increase opportunities for black-owned businesses and suppliers. The move sparked a national boycott led by black activists, including Pastor Jamal Bryant and Jaylani Hussein, which began with a 40-day "Target Fast" campaign. The boycott continued for about a year before organizers announced in March 2026 that it was ending.

The retailer had previously positioned itself as a major supporter of black-owned brands. Target pledged in 2021 to invest $2 billion in black-owned businesses by the end of 2025, and had programs aimed at expanding the number of black-owned brands on its shelves.

He revealed how transformational support can unlock potential across all sectors and explained why the science community in particular stands to benefit from this powerful practice.

Fuller's path to coaching wasn't planned - it emerged organically from years of facilitating conversations and creating spaces where people felt comfortable being vulnerable. The turning point came during a roundtable discussion when a professional from the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) posed a simple question: "Have you ever considered coaching?"

"I was told I had a skillset that makes people feel comfortable, open, and vulnerable - both from a technical and personal perspective," Fuller recalled. "That was the real recognition moment. Maybe I should do something here."

The suggestion wasn't isolated. Colleagues who had observed his facilitation work, podcasting, and webinar moderation consistently noted his natural ability to draw out authentic responses and create psychological safety. But Fuller explained how he needed to understand why.

A tapestry of experience

He reflected on his background and identified a unique convergence of skills developed across seemingly disparate careers. Growing up performing in church, he learned to speak confidently and connect with audiences. His time in the music industry taught him about creative expression and collaboration. As an educator, he discovered how to support individuals within groups while managing large-scale productions. Recruitment honed his ability to ask open questions that elicit meaningful information. And community work - "the first cousin of DEI," as he calls it - deepened his understanding of representation and belonging.

"If key professionals I respect are complimenting me on these abilities," Fuller reasoned, "maybe I should pursue this formally."

Harvard thought changing the words would save them.

But the words never mattered according to a new IRS rule.

And Donald Trump's Treasury just told 18,000 colleges that the woke rebrand is over.

The Scheme Bessent Just Exposed

These schools had a plan after the Supreme Court killed race-based admissions in 2023.

Stop saying "racial preferences" and start saying "equity," "inclusion," and "diversity-enhancing practices."

Same thumb on the scale, just with new vocabulary.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called it exactly what it is.

"Under President Trump, this Administration is standing up for America's students by ensuring racial discrimination has no place in American education," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. "Schools rebranding race-based preferences as equitable, inclusive, or diversity-enhancing does not change their discriminatory nature."

IRS Chief Executive Frank Bisignano made the consequences clear.

"Private educational institutions that promote discriminatory practices will no longer be afforded the benefits of federal tax-exempt status," Bisignano said. "Today's proposed regulations put institutions on notice and schools that continue to engage in racial discrimination should expect to lose that status."

About 18,000 private schools - from elite universities down to trade schools - are now on the clock.

"Under the proposed rule, a private school would not qualify for Federal tax-exempt status under section 501(c)(3) if it adopts, maintains, or enforces a policy or practice that discriminates on the basis of race, color, or national or ethnic origin," a press release stated. "The rule would apply across admissions, educational policies, scholarships and loans, athletics, and every other school-administered or school-supported program."

The rule takes effect May 31, 2027.

The Left Cheered This Exact Move Once

Here is the part that should make your blood boil.

This has happened before.

In 1976, the IRS stripped Bob Jones University in South Carolina of its tax-exempt status for banning interracial dating.

Bob Jones fought back all the way to the Supreme Court.

After years of heated debate, the American Bar Association's accreditation council is scheduled to make a final decision Tuesday on whether it will repeal a decades-old standard that requires law schools to "demonstrate by concrete action a commitment to diversity and inclusion."

Critics say the policy must go because it violates the Supreme Court's 2023 decision banning the consideration of race in admissions. But supporters, including a number of law school deans and faculty members, say that view applies an overreaching interpretation of the court's order. Ensuring diversity in the legal sector is critical to the health of American democracy, some proponents say, since attorneys -- who are often architects and enforcers of the law -- should accurately represent the demographics of the national population.

The council's vote takes place amid ongoing attacks by the Trump administration on both diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives and accreditors more broadly. It also comes two weeks after the Department of Education recommended that ABA's council, formally called the Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar, be denied federal recognition -- in part because of its diversity criterion.

Known as Standard 206, the accreditation council's quality metric for an inclusive student body has gone through several iterations, beginning in the 1970s and early 1980s -- when civil rights groups and the federal government were pressuring law schools to address their overwhelmingly white, male student bodies and affirmative action was at its prime. The council later added a second subsection requiring a similar commitment to diversity in the composition of faculty and staff.

The Trump administration's recommendation to discontinue the ABA accreditation council's federal recognition does not directly denounce the language of Standard 206. But the White House chastised the ABA and its diversity criterion specifically in the April 2025 executive order titled "Reforming Accreditation to Strengthen Higher Education," which says, "This standard and similar unlawful mandates must be permanently eradicated."

Some higher education experts say a vote to repeal the standard will signify Trump's ability to use federal recognition as a political lever to bring a powerful accreditor to heel.

In an interview with Inside Higher Ed, the accreditation council's chair, Melissa Hart, stressed that the group is considering the repeal of Standard 206 for multiple reasons, including that it conflicts with a number of state laws and court decisions. As a result, she explained, maintaining the DEI standard could prevent ABA accreditation from being recognized as a portable path to attorney licensure in all 50 states -- something state supreme courts have told her they don't want to happen.

It is a story that has its roots in the centuries that Curcuraci renews every first Sunday of September. A devotion deeply linked to the territory and to the figure of the Madonna dei Bianchi, a title that also recalls the tradition of the Virgin of Montalto, the "White Lady" of Messina's religious history. This year's celebration, on the centenary of the foundation of the parish, had the flavor of a tradition that is renewed without losing its connection with the past. Alongside the historic group of bearers, in fact, it was once again the young people who ideally took up the baton, participating with enthusiasm in the procession and becoming protagonists of that generational transition which allows an ancient devotion to continue to live.

The parish priest, Don Gianmarco Restuccia, will lead the moments of the celebration and, since last year, has chosen to increasingly involve the children of the community, together with the celebration committee and with the support of the Sixth Municipality. The novena accompanied the faithful in the days preceding the celebration, alternating moments of prayer with opportunities for meeting and conviviality. A celebration conceived not only as a religious event, but as a moment capable of bringing the entire community together around its roots. Among the most significant initiatives was the curcuracense harvest festival, in collaboration with the CISL Messina, in which the community was the protagonist of the pressing of the grapes and the preparation of the mustard. The most intense moment came at the end of the Eucharistic celebration, presided over by the provincial minister of the Friars Minor, Brother Antonino Catalfamo.

By Kellie Ell

Australia's broking industry turned its attention to diversity on Tuesday.

The Mortgage and Finance Association of Australia's (MFAA) hosted its biennial event, the 2026 "Diversity, Equity and Inclusion Summit," at The Collider in Sydney's Haymarket suburb with roughly a hundred people in attendance. The event was in partnership with Liberty and Mortgage Choice.

Speakers included MFAA Chief Executive Officer Anja Pannek, Liberty Financial's Chief People Officer Anne Bastian, REA Group's General Counsel Financial Services Scott Stierli, and the Australian Human Rights Commission's Race Discrimination Commissioner Giridharan Sivaraman. Shirley Chowdhary served as MC of the event.

Opening the summit, Pannek reflected on the industry's first DEI summit, and the progress the industry has made since.

"Two years ago, in 2024, we came together as part of the first DEI summit for our industry. And on that day I said I hoped it would be the start of what we would see as a real shift on the importance of DEI and how we thought about inclusivity for our industry. This is about the future sustainability of our industry," Pannek said. "And I think, if we fast forward two years [ago] to now, that conversation is more important than ever. DEI in 2026, like I said in 2024, it's not about a label; it's not about a trend."

Guests included brokers, lenders, aggregators and other senior-level executives from National Australia Bank (NAB), Westpac, AFG, non-bank lender MA Money, Finsure and more. The afternoon program also featured a series of breakout sessions.

This year's summit was centred on the theme of "opening doors", which the CEO said carried particular relevance in the current environment.

"Brokers open doors," Pannek said. "They open the first door for a homeowner. They open, maybe, the next house as a family changes, as something in their circumstances changes. Or they open a door for a business to grow and employ more people.

"Which leads me to the question, and why we're here today, which is: if we're really good at opening doors for Australians, are we equally as good at opening doors for people in this industry?" she continued. Christian music has produced countless songs that inspire faith, offer comfort, and give voice to moments of gratitude, struggle, surrender, and hope. The most beloved Christian songs combine memorable melodies with powerful messages about grace, redemption, perseverance, worship, and the presence of God. From timeless hymns and gospel influenced classics to contemporary worship anthems and modern Christian pop, these songs have connected with listeners across generations and denominations. Some are quiet prayers, while others rise into soaring declarations meant for entire congregations to sing together. Their lasting power comes from honest emotion and the ability to turn deeply personal faith into a shared musical experience.

1. I Can Only Imagine by MercyMe

MercyMe's I Can Only Imagine became one of the defining Christian songs of the modern era because it approaches the idea of heaven through wonder rather than certainty. Written by MercyMe frontman Bart Millard, the song imagines what a believer might experience when finally standing in the presence of Jesus. Instead of trying to describe heaven in elaborate detail, Millard repeatedly admits that he can only imagine the moment. That humility gives the song much of its emotional strength.

The arrangement begins gently, allowing Millard's warm vocal to carry the central questions. Would someone dance, remain still, sing praise, fall to their knees, or find themselves unable to speak? The song never chooses one answer. As the instrumentation grows, those questions become increasingly powerful because the listener has time to place personal faith, grief, hope, and expectation inside them. The recording became especially meaningful for people dealing with bereavement, giving Christian audiences a musical language for imagining reunion beyond death.

MercyMe developed a substantial catalog beyond this signature recording. Word of God Speak explores the desire for quiet spiritual intimacy, while Even If focuses on maintaining faith when circumstances do not improve. Greater delivers a more energetic message of confidence, and Flawless centers on grace and transformation. The band's ability to combine accessible pop rock songwriting with openly Christian themes helped them reach listeners well beyond traditional worship settings.

I Can Only Imagine remains their most universally recognized song because it asks questions many believers have considered privately. Its melody is simple enough to feel immediate, but the subject is enormous. MercyMe created a song about eternity that never pretends to possess all the answers, and that sense of awe has allowed it to remain deeply personal to millions of listeners.

It is often said in China that anyone who wants to understand Chinese politics should read "Dream of the Red Chamber," an 18th-century epic novel, which depicts the rise and fall of an old, aristocratic clan.

I read it. The complexity of human relations was something that left a lasting impression on me, as did the sheer opulence in which the protagonists lived.

One outstanding example of that had to do with how an eggplant dish was prepared.

"It's not difficult at all," insisted the character, who explained the procedure at great length.

Eggplants are chopped and fried in chicken fat. Dried tofu, seasoned with bamboo shoots, "shiitake" mushrooms, Sichuan pepper, star anise and cinnamon, is simmered in chicken broth.

The broth is poured over the chopped eggplant, then the whole concoction goes into a ceramic bottle and the bottle is sealed.

I wouldn't mind tasting it. But then, the eggplant doesn't need all that work to be delectable.

In her elegant prose, author Aya Koda (1904-1990) wrote to the effect: "Wash a cucumber, an eggplant and 'myoga' (Japanese ginger), dice them all rhythmically with a knife, add a dash of 'shoyu' and stir. Now, you are all ready for the coolness."

Author Tsutomu Mizukami (1919-2004) favored the eggplant, calling it "the king of the summer vegetable garden." He said he liked it best when it was freshly harvested from his garden, steamed, with ginger added later, and flavored with shoyu. "This is the taste of the earth."

With the prices of so many food items skyrocketing because of the recent extreme weather, the eggplant is to be much appreciated for its daily presence on the dining table.

Even if one doesn't go so far as to consult "Dream of the Red Chamber," it is still human nature, I think, to blindly want something "unusual" and make some extra effort that may not even be necessary.

But having grown older -- although not necessarily wiser -- I have come to truly appreciate the preciousness of just being myself.

Yesterday was "Hakuro" (White Dew), one of the 24 solar terms in the traditional East Asian calendar. This is said to be the day when one begins to feel the autumn season for real.

A haiku by Junya Ishii goes to the effect, "Autumn rain came quietly/ A horse figurine fashioned from an eggplant."

I ate many eggplants this summer. I look forward to enjoying them in autumn.

-- The Asahi Shimbun, Sept. 8

MADISON, Wis. -- Even though he was nearly 2,000 miles from where he'd grown up, Ryan Hopkins felt right at home as a quarterback prospect visiting Wisconsin.

"I felt the energy from the city," said Hopkins, a former three-star recruit from Mater Dei in Santa Ana, Calif. "I felt the energy from the coaches."

But there was a complication that went beyond the distance factor. Hopkins had to deal with the dilemma facing just about every high school quarterback prospect since most Bowl Subdivision programs now overwhemingly rely on transfers at that position: About 65% of the FBS starting quarterbacks to open this season transferred at some point in their careers.

"It's a totally different ballgame," said Trent Dilfer, who has experienced quarterback recruiting from just about every angle.

Dilfer is a former Fresno State quarterback and first-round draft pick who started for the Baltimore Ravens' Super Bowl championship team in the 2000 season. He coached a high school power at Lipscomb Academy in Nashville, Tenn., was a college head coach at Alabama-Birmingham and now is back at Lipscomb.

He remembers when a quarterback coming out of high school could learn on the job. Colleges don't need to be that patient anymore because so many college quarterbacks with starting experience are available each year since the NCAA erased the requirement of sitting out a year before the 2021-22 season.

"And that changed everything," Dilfer said. "Because instead of recruiting the child, now you're recruiting a man."

Hopkins chose Wisconsin even as the Badgers enter a fourth straight season with a transfer as their starting quarterback. Hopkins spent the summer competing with Louisville transfer Deuce Adams for the right to back up Old Dominion transfer Colton Joseph, who got the start in the Badgers' season-opening loss to No. 4 Notre Dame on Sunday night.

THE NEW NORM

The reliance on transfers by most major programs leaves fewer roster spots available for high school prospects.

"If you're a quarterback in this day and age, you have to earn it and you have to say, 'I'm OK with taking less when I'm first getting recruited, because I want to get more when I show how good I am,' " Washington Coach Jedd Fisch said.
